title: Love stays
hookLine: a father ran from his sick daughter's bedside, calling it love; Epictetus questions him gently (Discourses 1.11)
carry: an ordinary chair pulled up beside a bed

lines: I JUST CAN'T SEE HER LIKE THAT.
cards: Some people can't do hospitals. The smell, the beeping, the sight of someone they love looking small in a bed. They say it with real pain: I just can't see her like that.

A Roman official said almost exactly that to Epictetus. His little daughter had been dangerously ill. He couldn't bear it, so he left the house and stayed away until someone came to tell him she was better.
He told the story as proof of how much he loved her.

teach.h: HE DOESN'T CALL HIM A COWARD.
teach.b: This is Discourses book one, chapter eleven, on natural affection. Notice how Epictetus handles it. He doesn't call the man a coward, and he doesn't doubt that he loves his daughter.
He asks a question: do you think you did right? It's natural, the father says. Every father feels this way.
All right, Epictetus says, let's test it.
If running away was the loving thing, then it would be loving for everyone who cares about her to do it: her mother, her nurse, her tutor. Picture them all, out of pure affection, leaving the house.
The little girl would be left alone, or with strangers who didn't care about her at all. Would you want that, he asks, if you were the one who was sick?

teach.h: IT WAS A JUDGMENT, NOT LOVE.
teach.b: Would you want the people who love you most to be the ones who leave? The father has to admit: no.
So it wasn't love that made you run, Epictetus says gently.
Love would have kept you there. Then what was it? The same thing behind every choice: it seemed right to you at the time.
A judgment. And judgments can be examined. It's a tender lesson.
Strong feeling isn't the same as love. Sometimes love looks like an ordinary chair pulled up beside a bed, someone sitting there who'd rather be anywhere else, and staying anyway.

how: People who take this chapter to heart often treat visiting the sick, or simply staying present with someone who is suffering, as a practice in its own right.

o: love means keeping the people you love from all pain
love shows in staying near, not in how strongly you feel
love is whatever feeling runs strongest in you

p: what if they all ran too?

s: Epictetus calls the father a coward
he never doubts the father's love; he questions whether running was loving.
he asks what would happen if everyone who loved the girl did the same
she'd be left alone or with strangers who didn't care.
Epictetus says the cause of the running was a judgment
it seemed right to him at the time, and judgments can be examined.

games.q: you're the father. your little girl is dangerously ill and you can't bear to see her. what did the father in the story do?
o: left the house until word came she was better.
games.why: he ran and stayed away, calling it love. Epictetus gently showed him that love would have stayed.

practice: Think of someone who is unwell, in body or in spirit, or who's going through something hard, and notice if part of you pulls away, the way the father did. Don't scold that part; just see it.
Then picture yourself pulling up a chair beside them, the way you'd want someone to sit beside you.

wordCard.voice: Love stays. Epictetus' gentle correction to a father who ran from his sick child: the feeling was strong, but love would have stayed.

orig.note: Greek philostorgia: tender family affection, the love of parents and children; the title word of Discourses 1.11.

carryVoice: Your line: an ordinary chair pulled up beside a bed. The feeling can run strong; love is what stays. Until tomorrow.
